title: ChatGPT-3.5, ChatGPT-4, Google Bard, and Microsoft Bing to Improve Health Literacy and Communication in Pediatric Populations and Beyond
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models can be used to improve health literacy by generating explanations of pediatric medical conditions at different reading-grade levels. The authors were interested in two related questions: whether models such as ChatGPT-3.5, ChatGPT-4, Google Bard, and Microsoft Bing can produce explanations from a basic prompt, and whether adding explicit reading-level instructions helps the models tailor output for younger readers.

To study this, the authors tested 288 childhood disorders and conditions using two basic prompts and two prompt styles that specified grade level, spanning first through twelfth grade. They evaluated the output with readability indices and word counts, comparing performance across models. The work was conducted using publicly available LLMs and did not involve human participants, instead focusing on the textual outputs generated by the systems.

The main finding was that all models struggled to consistently generate truly low-grade reading levels, especially below sixth grade. ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4 showed the greatest ability to vary output by requested grade level, while Bing and Bard tended to stay closer to high-school-level readability. The authors conclude that LLMs have promise for generating patient education materials for pediatric audiences, but current models are limited in their ability to precisely target easy reading levels and should be used cautiously alongside other educational tools.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational large language model chatbot system used to generate and adapt text responses.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper evaluated ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4 on their ability to explain pediatric medical conditions at different reading-grade levels in response to basic and grade-specified prompts.

findings.finding_summary: Across 288 childhood conditions, ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4 produced outputs that could be shifted toward lower reading-grade levels when prompts specified grade level, but neither model reliably matched the requested target. For basic prompts, both models produced college-level text at baseline; with 'Explain {} to a __ grader' and 'Explain {} at a __-grade reading level' prompts, ChatGPT-3.5 ranged roughly from 6th/7th grade to college-freshmen/twelfth-grade levels and ChatGPT-4 ranged from about 6th grade to college-senior level, depending on prompt wording.
findings.measure: Average reading grade level (aRGL) of generated explanations; word count
findings.sample_size: n=288 conditions; ChatGPT-4 tested on n=150 conditions

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google's conversational large language model chatbot system (formerly Bard) used to generate text responses.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper evaluated Google Bard on its ability to explain pediatric medical conditions at different reading-grade levels in response to basic and grade-specified prompts.

findings.finding_summary: Google Bard generally produced high-school-level text and showed limited ability to precisely adapt to requested reading grade levels. Across prompts, Bard ranged from about 7th to 10th grade on grade-specified prompts, tended to stay near the high-school level, and failed to generate responses for some conditions on basic prompts (e.g., 11 failures for 'What is/are' and 19 failures for 'Explain').
findings.measure: Average reading grade level (aRGL) of generated explanations; word count; rate of failed outputs

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic large language model / chatbot system used for generating and simplifying text at different reading levels.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as a generic category label for the study's evaluation of large language model outputs for health-literacy-oriented explanations, although the paper actually named specific products.

findings.finding_summary: The study found that LLM outputs could be adjusted somewhat by prompt specificity, but models struggled to consistently produce text below a sixth-grade reading level. The overall conclusion was that generative AI showed promise for tailoring patient education materials, while remaining limited in exact grade-level control and in some cases refusing to answer prompts.
findings.measure: Reading grade level of outputs; word count; prompt success/failure

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational large language model chatbot system used to generate and adapt text responses.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper also evaluated ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4 on word count variation across prompts and the relationship between prompt grade level and output length/readability.

findings.finding_summary: ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4 showed increasing word count as requested grade level increased in some prompt structures, but the relationship between word count and readability was inconsistent across prompts. ChatGPT-4 generally produced longer outputs than ChatGPT-3.5, with the study noting greater variation in word count for OpenAI models than for Bing or Bard.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a single descriptive evaluation of LLM output readability, not an experimental intervention study or meta-analysis. It provides useful comparative information but does not meet higher-evidence design standards.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests practical potential for tailoring reading level, but it reports no effect sizes and no direct learner outcomes. Impact is therefore suggestive and modest rather than demonstrated.
